Add a distinct genre classification for Islamic mourning recitation (Noha / Marsiya). Introduce a dedicated genre value for Islamic mourning recitation, so this material is classified separately from music and is not treated as music by playback and recommendation features. Why this is a product problem, not a content one: Noha, Marsiya, Soz and Salaam are liturgical lamentation recited during periods of mourning, principally Muharram and Safar, in Shia Muslim communities worldwide. They are not consumed as entertainment. They are performed and listened to in a state of grief, often communally. This content is already on Spotify in large volume. The problem is that no accurate genre value exists in the ingestion taxonomy, so distributors are forced to deliver it under Pop, World, Devotional or similar. The consequences for listeners are concrete: 1. Autoplay follows a noha with upbeat music, because the audio-features model reads the recitation as a slow track with a crowd vocal and selects neighbours accordingly. The transition is genuinely distressing in context. 2. Mourning listening contaminates Discover Weekly, daylist and Wrapped, surfacing lamentation as light listening the rest of the year. 3. Search and browse cannot distinguish lamentation from celebratory devotional forms such as Manqabat, which are liturgically opposite and should never be interleaved. A correct genre value at ingestion resolves all three, because it gives recommendation, autoplay and editorial systems a signal they currently do not have. It also gives distributors something accurate to select at delivery, rather than defaulting to whatever is closest on their list. Scope: one taxonomy addition. Related forms (Marsiya, Soz, Salaam, Manqabat) can sit under it as sub-values or be handled separately later; this request is for the parent genre only. Who this affects: listeners across Pakistan, India, Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Lebanon, Azerbaijan, and large diaspora populations in the Gulf, Europe, North America and Australia; a listener base that is already paying for Spotify and currently has no accurate way to listen to this material on it. I would be glad to help compile evidence on current mis-tagging across artists in this space if that is useful to the relevant team
